title: Your First Pod
intro: Let's create your first pod. In real k8s, you'd use kubectl run for a quick one-off pod.

steps.prompt: Create a pod named 'my-first-pod' using the nginx image.
steps.explanation: kubectl run creates a single pod directly — no Deployment, no self-healing. Good for quick tests, not production.
steps.why: kubectl run is for one-off pods. For anything long-lived you'd use 'kubectl create deployment' or 'kubectl apply -f' instead, since only a Deployment notices when a pod dies and replaces it.

steps.fake_output:
NAME            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
my-first-pod    1/1     Running   0          5s
steps.explanation: kubectl get pods lists everything in the current namespace.
steps.why: 'kubectl get pod my-first-pod' (singular, named) works just as well and is more precise once you know the name — 'get pods' (plural) is better when you're scanning everything in the namespace.

steps.prompt: Look at the full details of the pod.
steps.fake_output:
Name: my-first-pod
Status: Running
IP: 10.244.0.5
Node: node-1
Containers:
  nginx:
    Image: nginx
    State: Running
steps.explanation: describe gives you the full picture — events, IP, container status, node it's on.
steps.why: 'kubectl get pod my-first-pod -o yaml' shows the same underlying object, but describe adds a human-readable Events section at the bottom — that's usually what you actually want when debugging.

steps.explanation: Since this pod wasn't managed by a Deployment, deleting it is final — nothing recreates it.
steps.why: There's no gentler alternative for a bare pod like this. If it were managed by a Deployment, you'd scale it to 0 or delete the Deployment instead — deleting just the pod would get it recreated immediately.
